sources.title: Matthew Restall: Invasion: The Maya at War, 1520s to 1540s
sources.note: Original scholarly chapter indexed text checked with query Restall Invasion 1527 1547. Section Where, When, and What: Four Regions, northern Yucatan paragraph. Direct PDF retrieval failed. Supports three Montejo invasions from 1527, Tihó/Mérida 1542, major northeastern revolt crushed in 1547, continued fluctuating frontier. No claim that all Maya peoples were conquered then.

sources.title: Douglas J. Kennett and colleagues: Drought-Induced Civil Conflict Among the Ancient Maya (2022)
sources.note: Direct original research article read. Introduction, Results and Discussion: Mayapán gates and residential gardens; 205 directly AMS-dated skeletons; climate and violence correlation; collapse about 1441 to 1461; enduring regional markets and smaller polities. Climate exacerbation is the authors’ multicausal interpretation, not deterministic proof.

sources.title: INAH: Tulum archaeological zone
sources.note: Direct indexed official archaeology entry: visible buildings generally 1250 to 1550, walls on three landward sides, five access points, two watchtowers, Caribbean eastern edge, murals and coastal connections. Spanish version /es/node/4361 is same source. No generalization from much earlier dated stela to all buildings.

sources.title: Elizabeth H. Paris: Metallurgy, Mayapan, and the Postclassic Mesoamerican World System (2008)
sources.note: Publisher abstract directly checked: excavated artifacts and casting debris demonstrate local lost-wax casting; imported metal and interregional exchange; access broader than an exclusively elite monopoly. Full article not claimed read.

sources.title: Diego de Landa: Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, modern Spanish transcription of the c.1566 account
sources.note: Full PDF directly read through Wayeb, European Association of Mayanists. PDF pages 16,41,43,62,86 to 87: priestly education, houses, food, children and month-Zip healing festival. Landa was a coercive colonial missionary; his account is attributed, selective and not treated as a neutral census. All four passages pooled under this single work.

sources.title: Susan D. deFrance and Craig A. Hanson: Labor, Population Movement, and Food in Sixteenth-Century Ek Balam, Yucatán
sources.note: Publisher abstract directly read: early Hispanic faunal feature; mid-sixteenth-century encomienda and Franciscan visita; local introduced pigs/chickens and continued prominence of indigenous dog meat. Site-specific conclusion, not a general Maya diet.

sources.title: Matthew Restall: He Wished It in Vain: Subordination and Resistance among Maya Women in Post-Conquest Yucatan (1995)
sources.note: Direct full scholarly PDF, printed 587 to 589 especially property and wills. Examples span mid-seventeenth through later colonial centuries; card explicitly identifies material after map endpoint. Women’s house plots, plants, animals, textiles, looms and clothing bequests.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: The Calendar System
sources.note: Direct original institutional page checked: 365-day Haab, 18 twenty-day months plus five days; 260-day Tzolkin combines twenty named days with thirteen numbers; Calendar Round 52 Haab years. Pooled conservatively with same-project modern Maya page.

sources.title: SLUB Dresden: Maya-Handschrift, Codex Dresdensis
sources.note: Direct indexed holding-library description checked: 39 leaves, 3.56 m folded strip of bark-fibre material, c.1300 to 1521 Yucatan, ritual and astronomical contents. Dates are library attribution, not an exact scribal colophon.

sources.title: Daniel G. Brinton, editor: The Maya Chronicles (1882), Chronicle of Chac Xulub Chen
sources.note: Original edition directly read. Printed 189 quotes u belil u kahlail Cħac Xulub Cħen and translation; §§39 to 41, printed 240 to 241, town land and inheritance claims. Historical Latin spelling preserved, including ħ; not presented as ancient hieroglyphs or modern standardized spelling. Brinton’s obsolete ethnological commentary and speculative etymology excluded.

sources.title: Newberry Library: Modern Editions of Colonial Spanish Sources, Linguistics bibliography, Ayer MS 1601
sources.note: Indexed original catalogue page 35: Códice Nakuk Pech, original work 1562; photographic copy of Juan Pío Pérez’s 1840 to 1859 manuscript copy. Distinguishes transmission from sixteenth-century autograph.

sources.title: INAH, Bulletin 367: Reconstruyen el auto de fe de Maní (26 June 2024)
sources.note: Indexed original institutional bulletin directly checked; direct retrieval failed. First-page heading and paragraphs: auto-da-fé 12 July 1562; 2015 rescue archaeology recovered 548 remains of vessels/incense burners identified by INAH with the destruction. Count means pieces/remains, not 548 complete objects. Web bulletin duplicate treated as same source.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: The Maya
sources.note: Indexed original page directly checked: contemporary Maya communities and more than thirty languages; Yucatec Maya archaeologist/architect José Huchim Herrera says Weyano’one, we are here. Only the bounded continuity material is used; dated population totals and broad claims about city abandonment omitted. Pooled with Calendar System as one institutional project.

proposedOverrides.summary: Maya communities of northern Yucatán during Spanish invasion and colonial transformation, with earlier cultural achievements and continuing lives.

batchIdentityNotes.index: Exact missing indexed HB record1530 to 1650. No aliases absorbed. Existingmaya card remains unchanged; maya-yucateco1492 to 1500 is related but distinct map phase; mayaimi is Florida and mayangna Nicaragua/Honduras.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded world1530/world1600 polygons: bbox -89.9991,17.6352,-86.8995,21.5896, northern/eastern Yucatan. Does not encompass all Maya peoples, including highland and southern communities. Public overview explicitly warns about identity, independence and rough frontier.
batchIdentityNotes.scope: Foregrounds sixteenth-century Yucatan. Mayapan,metalworking,Tulum andcodex each receive explicit dates/context; laterwills and contemporaryvoices explicitly later. No unsupported toilets/medical efficacy/universal schooling. Moderncardkindculture prevents invented single empire.
batchIdentityNotes.separateDefect: Existing maya ID contains Australian namesake polygons from1600 onward; root notified for separate geometry repair. This packet does not alter that record or use its late polygons.
